items.title: Trial status change: NCT07435298 is now 'Suspended'
items.whyMatters: The registry entry for this trial moved from 'Recruiting' to 'Suspended'. Status changes are verified directly against ClinicalTrials.gov.
items.summary: Navigated rTMS for chronic tinnitus — sponsor National University Hospital, Singapore. Status verified at the registry on 2026-09-26.

items.title: Tympanometry fails as a screening test for finding the cause of pulsatile tinnitus
items.whyMatters: Some clinics hoped a simple ear-pressure test could tell which pulsatile tinnitus patients need a scan; this review of 107 patients found the test was little better than a coin flip. If you have pulsatile tinnitus, a normal tympanometry result should not be used as a reason to skip imaging.
items.summary: First reasonably sized evaluation of ambient pressure tympanometry (APT) as a bedside screening test for finding a radiologic cause of subjective pulsatile tinnitus — and it performs poorly (sensitivity ~43–57%, specificity ~54–57%), essentially no better than chance. This is diagnostic-workup evidence, not treatment evidence. 63/137 ears (46%) had a pulse-synchronous APT pattern; 51 (37.2%) had a radiologic correlate; 65 (44.2%) received a surgeon diagnosis. For a radiologic correlate: sensitivity 51%, specificity 57%, PPV 41.3%, NPV 66.2%. For a surgeon diagnosis: sensitivity 43.1%, specificity 54.9%, PPV 43.1%, NPV 54.9%. Chief-complaint subgroup (116 ears): radiologic correlate 56.9%/54.2%/46%/55.2%; surgeon diagnosis 43.6%/54.1%/46.2%/51.6%.

detail.population: Adults with subjective pulsatile tinnitus evaluated at a tertiary otolaryngology clinic (Mayo Clinic Florida) who underwent ambient pressure tympanometry between 2021 and 2025; 137 of 147 ears also had imaging
detail.sampleSize: 107 patients (147 ears); 137 ears imaged; subgroup of 86 patients (116 ears) whose chief complaint was pulsatile tinnitus
detail.primaryEndpoint: Sensitivity and specificity of a pulse-synchronous APT tracing for detecting a radiologic correlate of pulsatile tinnitus (two reference standards: any radiologic diagnosis, and surgeon-defined diagnosis)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Positive and negative predictive values; same metrics in the subgroup whose chief complaint was pulsatile tinnitus
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is a diagnostic accuracy study; no tinnitus loudness was measured or treated.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life outcomes were assessed.
detail.safety: Not reported — no interventions were administered; APT and imaging safety were not discussed.
limitations: Retrospective single-institution chart review with tertiary referral bias
Imperfect reference standards — 'radiologic correlate' and 'surgeon diagnosis' are themselves subjective and imperfect, and imaging protocols likely varied
Ears rather than patients treated as units of analysis (clustering within patients)
No confidence intervals or prevalence-adjusted predictive values reported in the abstract
10 ears had no imaging; verification bias possible
No tinnitus severity, loudness or outcome measures at all
detail.funding: independent — 'Conflict of interest statement: None declared'; academic centers (Mayo Clinic Florida, Geisinger), no manufacturer funding disclosed.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Two case reports describe stellate ganglion pulsed radiofrequency for tinnitus
items.whyMatters: Two patients had a nerve-block-style procedure in the neck and reported less tinnitus distress two months later, which is an unusual approach worth watching. But two uncontrolled cases cannot show that a treatment works — improvements of this kind often happen with placebo or simply over time, and the procedure is invasive.
items.summary: A single-author case report describes two patients with long-standing tinnitus treated with pulsed radiofrequency of the stellate ganglion plus local anesthetic and corticosteroid, with reported reductions in self-described tinnitus intensity and THI at 2 months. The anatomical target (cervical sympathetic chain) is novel for tinnitus, but the evidence level is the lowest possible — two uncontrolled anecdotes. No numeric values given in the abstract: THI reportedly fell from the 'catastrophic' band to the 'moderate' band in both cases, and tinnitus intensity was described as decreased at 2 months. No loudness-match decibel values, no VAS numbers, no statistics (N=2).

detail.population: Two adults with long-standing (chronic) subjective tinnitus and catastrophic baseline THI scores, treated in a Spanish pain medicine department; no further demographic, etiologic, audiometric or laterality detail available in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — case reports have no prespecified endpoint; narrative outcomes were tinnitus intensity and Tinnitus Handicap Inventory at approximately 2 months
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — 'intensity decreased' is an uncontrolled subjective impression in two patients with no psychoacoustic loudness matching, no blinding and no comparator, so this provides no usable evidence about the tinnitus percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: limited — THI dropping from catastrophic to moderate in two patients is anecdotal and entirely consistent with placebo response, natural fluctuation, regression to the mean after presentation at a peak of severity, and reporting bias toward positive cases.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported — no sleep, quality-of-life, hearing, anxiety/depression or audiometric outcomes described.
detail.safety: The report states the procedure was well tolerated with no adverse events in the two treated patients; follow-up was approximately 2 months. This is far too small a sample to characterize the known risks of stellate ganglion intervention (Horner syndrome, hoarseness, dysphagia, intravascular or intrathecal injection, pneumothorax) or of corticosteroid exposure.
limitations: N=2 case series — the weakest design for efficacy inference
No control, no sham, no randomization, no blinding
Within-patient before/after comparison only; placebo and regression to the mean uncontrolled
Publication/selection bias: successful cases are the ones written up
Short follow-up (~2 months), no durability data
Combined intervention (pulsed RF + local anesthetic + corticosteroid) — the active component cannot be identified
No psychoacoustic loudness matching; 'intensity' undefined and unquantified
No numeric THI values, no patient characteristics, no tinnitus etiology or hearing status reported
Single author, single center, case-report journal with limited methodological scrutiny
Invasive procedure with real (if uncommon) risks that cannot be assessed at this sample size
detail.funding: independent — the author declares no conflicts of interest; no manufacturer funding or device sponsorship is disclosed, and no funding statement is visible in the record.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Norwegian uncontrolled study: internet-delivered TRT plus CBT linked to modest tinnitus distress improvement over six months
items.whyMatters: An online program combining tinnitus retraining therapy and CBT was followed in 144 Norwegian patients, who reported modest reductions in tinnitus-related distress over six months, with the biggest change in those who started out most severely affected. Because there was no comparison group, this cannot show how much of the improvement came from the treatment itself, and it says nothing about how loud the tinnitus sounds.
items.summary: A Norwegian naturalistic (uncontrolled, single-arm) service-evaluation of an internet-delivered program combining tinnitus retraining therapy and CBT in 144 patients, reporting THI change to 180 days with effect sizes stratified by baseline severity (largest change in the severe+ group). The severity-stratified reporting is the main novel element; the overall finding that guided digital CBT-type programs reduce tinnitus distress is already well established by controlled trials. THI pre-treatment to 180 days: d = 0.41 for the total sample; d = 0.95 for severe+ tinnitus; d = 0.22 for mild tinnitus. Small improvements in anxiety, depression and hyperacusis; no change in misophonia. Absolute THI point changes, confidence intervals, and attrition not given in the abstract.

detail.population: Patients diagnosed with tinnitus (primarily tinnitus as presenting complaint) receiving an internet-based TRT+CBT treatment in Norway; baseline severity ranged from mild to severe+ on THI
detail.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) from pre-treatment to 180 days
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Hyperacusis, misophonia, depression and anxiety symptom measures (instruments not specified in the abstract); 90-day assessment point
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — only THI and psychological questionnaires were used; no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was reported, so this says nothing about the tinnitus percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: limited — a moderate within-group THI improvement (d=0.41 overall, d=0.95 in the severe+ subgroup) with no control arm, so natural course, regression to the mean (especially in the severe+ subgroup selected on high baseline scores) and expectancy cannot be separated from treatment effect.
detail.otherOutcomes: Small improvements in self-reported anxiety, depression and hyperacusis; no change in misophonia. No sleep, quality-of-life or audiometric outcomes reported in the abstract.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse events, symptom worsening rates, or dropout-for-harm data described in the abstract.
limitations: No control or comparison group — within-group change only; natural history, regression to the mean and expectancy effects are unquantified
Not randomized, not blinded, naturalistic service-evaluation design
Severity-stratified subgroup effects (severe+ d=0.95) are especially prone to regression to the mean because groups were defined by baseline THI
Attrition/completion rates at 90 and 180 days not reported in the abstract; possible completer-only analysis
Follow-up limited to 180 days from treatment start; no longer-term durability data
No psychoacoustic or loudness outcome; intervention content, dose, adherence and degree of clinician guidance not specified in the abstract
Identity and ownership of the digital platform used are not clear from the abstract, so independence from a product vendor cannot be fully confirmed
detail.funding: independent — authors (university psychology department and a hospital ENT department) declare no commercial or financial relationships; funding source and the commercial status of the digital platform are not stated in the record, so vendor independence is not fully verifiable.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Protocol published for a small uncontrolled acupuncture study using brainstem-response recordings in chronic tinnitus
items.whyMatters: This is a plan for a future study, not results — and the acupuncture part has no placebo or comparison group, so it will not be able to show whether acupuncture works. Its more interesting idea is testing whether a brainstem hearing measurement can serve as an objective tinnitus marker, which the field currently lacks.
items.summary: A study protocol (no results) for an exploratory two-part study in China: a matched case-control comparison of auditory brainstem response (ABR) parameters in 36 chronic tinnitus patients vs 36 healthy controls, plus a single-arm, uncontrolled 10-session acupuncture course with THI/TEQ/VAS and ABR outcomes. Nothing is reported yet beyond design; the novelty is the attempt to pair acupuncture symptom change with an objective electrophysiological measure. none reported (protocol only; no outcome data)

detail.population: Adults with bilateral chronic tinnitus (n=36) and age- and sex-matched healthy controls (n=36), single centre, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University affiliated hospital, China
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not clearly designated; stated aims are ABR parameter differences between tinnitus patients and healthy controls, and change in ABR plus clinical measures after 10 acupuncture sessions over 4 weeks
detail.secondaryEndpoints: THI, Tinnitus Impact Questionnaire (TEQ), Tinnitus-Related Visual Analog Scale at baseline, post-treatment and 8-week follow-up; ABR test-retest variability in controls
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching is planned, and no data exist yet; the tinnitus-related VAS is a subjective rating collected without any control arm, and ABR is not a measure of percept loudness.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI/TEQ are planned but unreported, and the single-arm uncontrolled design could not attribute any future distress change to acupuncture rather than natural course, regression to the mean or placebo effects.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse event data are presented in this protocol publication.
limitations: Protocol only — no results reported
Intervention component is single-arm, self-controlled, with no sham or waitlist control
Not randomized and not blinded; strong susceptibility to placebo and natural-fluctuation effects in a subjective condition
Small planned sample (36 treated patients) for an exploratory endpoint
No psychoacoustic loudness matching; percept outcomes limited to subjective VAS
ABR is an unvalidated surrogate for tinnitus presence or severity; baseline group difference does not establish treatment mechanism
Single centre, acupuncture-specialist institution — enthusiasm/allegiance bias plausible even without commercial funding
Short 8-week follow-up
No published results to verify against registry NCT07522567
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no commercial or financial relationships; however all authors are based at a Chinese traditional-medicine university and its acupuncture department, an institutional allegiance worth noting.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Animal study: mTOR inhibitor everolimus reduces tinnitus-like behavior and cortical hyperactivity in rats
items.whyMatters: This is early laboratory work in rats suggesting that a brain-plasticity pathway (mTOR) may help drive tinnitus-related overactivity, and that an existing cancer/transplant drug can dampen it. It is a mechanism finding only — there is no human evidence, and everolimus has serious side effects, so it should not be viewed as a potential treatment today.
items.summary: First report that systemic everolimus (an approved mTOR inhibitor) reduces salicylate-induced tinnitus-like gap-detection deficits in rats while normalizing auditory cortex spontaneous firing, gamma power, theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, BDNF/PSD95 and glutamate levels. It extends the mTOR/maladaptive-plasticity hypothesis of tinnitus to a repurposable clinical drug, but entirely in an acute animal model. none reported (abstract gives directional findings only: EVE 'mitigated' gap-detection deficits and 'attenuated' elevated SFR, gamma power, theta-gamma PAC, BDNF/PSD95 and glutamate; no effect sizes, p-values or group sizes in the available record)

detail.population: Adult rats (strain not specified in abstract) with acute sodium salicylate-induced tinnitus-like behavior; three groups: Control, Tinnitus, Tinnitus+everolimus
detail.primaryEndpoint: Gap prepulse inhibition of the acoustic startle (GPIAS) as a behavioral proxy for tinnitus-like perception
detail.secondaryEndpoints: A1 spontaneous firing rates, gamma-band LFP power, theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling, c-Fos, mTOR pathway activation, BDNF and PSD95 expression, LC-MS/MS glutamate and other neurotransmitter levels
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — GPIAS in rats is a behavioral proxy for the presence of a tinnitus-like percept, not a human loudness measure; no psychoacoustic loudness matching exists here and no inference about human percept loudness can be drawn.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no distress, THI/TFI, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life outcomes are measurable in this preclinical design.
detail.otherOutcomes: Mechanistic/neurophysiological only: normalization of cortical hyperexcitability markers and glutamate accumulation. Hearing thresholds and possible salicylate-independent effects not reported in the abstract.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse-event, weight, immunosuppression or ototoxicity data appear in the available record; everolimus is known clinically to cause stomatitis, immunosuppression, metabolic and pulmonary toxicity, none of which were assessed here.
limitations: Animal study; acute salicylate model does not represent chronic human tinnitus
Sample sizes per group not reported
Randomization and blinding of behavioral/electrophysiological assessment not described
GPIAS is a contested proxy — salicylate also alters startle and hearing, which can confound gap detection
No dose-response, no long-term follow-up, no recovery/persistence data
No safety or tolerability assessment of a drug with known systemic toxicity
No numerical effect sizes available in the record
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing interests; academic Chinese hospital/university groups; funding source not stated in the available record. Note the journal is an open-access Dove Medical Press title, so peer-review rigor is variable.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Survey of 390 nursing-home residents links higher perceived social support to lower tinnitus handicap scores
items.whyMatters: Among older people living in care facilities, those who felt better supported by family and staff reported less tinnitus-related handicap — but because everything was measured at one point in time, this cannot show that more support reduces tinnitus rather than that less distressed people feel better supported. It measures distress and disability, not how loud the tinnitus is.
items.summary: A cross-sectional survey of 390 long-term-care residents aged 60+ with chronic subjective tinnitus in Wuhan, China reports that higher perceived social support (SSA-13) is associated with lower THI scores, adding institutionalized older adults to the literature on psychosocial correlates of tinnitus distress. It is an association study, not a treatment study, and provides no evidence that increasing social support reduces tinnitus. Per 1-SD higher SSA-13: adjusted THI 5.24 points lower (95% CI -7.34 to -3.14; p<0.001); adjusted OR for severe/catastrophic THI 0.60 (95% CI 0.45–0.80; p<0.001). Highest vs lowest SSA-13 quartile: adjusted β = -12.11 (95% CI -17.39 to -6.84), with non-monotonic intermediate quartiles and significant spline nonlinearity (p<0.001). Hypertension in the fully adjusted model: adjusted β = +23.82 (95% CI 19.00–28.65; p<0.001).

detail.population: Residents aged 60 years or older with chronic subjective tinnitus living in long-term care facilities in urban Wuhan, China (mean age 79.85, SD 8.32; 60.8% female), surveyed July–November 2025
detail.primaryEndpoint: Continuous Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) total score; severe/catastrophic THI analyzed as a binary secondary outcome
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Ordinal THI severity category and moderate-or-worse THI in sensitivity analyses; quartile, restricted cubic spline and subgroup analyses of SSA-13
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed; THI measures handicap/distress and says nothing about the loudness of the percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI differences here are cross-sectional associations between two self-report measures collected at the same time, not a treatment effect, so no distress benefit can be attributed to any intervention.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported — no sleep, hearing, or quality-of-life outcomes reported separately in the abstract
detail.safety: Not reported — observational survey with no intervention and no adverse-event reporting
limitations: Cross-sectional design: cannot establish direction of causality (distressed residents may perceive less support, rather than the reverse)
Single-city convenience setting (urban Wuhan long-term care facilities), limiting generalizability
Both exposure and outcome are self-report instruments measured at the same visit, inviting common-method and negative-affectivity bias
No adjustment reported for depression/anxiety, which plausibly drives both perceived support and THI
Implausibly large hypertension coefficient (+23.82 THI points) raises concern about model specification, residual confounding, or overfitting with many covariates
Non-monotonic quartile estimates and significant spline nonlinearity suggest an unstable dose-response relationship
No loudness, audiometric, or tinnitus-percept measures reported
No treatment tested; no control group, no randomization, no follow-up
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no commercial or financial relationships; no funder disclosed in the record (funding source unable to verify from this abstract)
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Scoping review maps noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation in ENT: tinnitus is the biggest but still exploratory evidence cluster
items.whyMatters: Researchers catalogued all human studies of non-surgical vagus nerve stimulation in ear, nose and throat conditions and found only 20, eight of them on tinnitus, all small and inconsistently designed. The authors conclude this treatment is not yet shown to work, which matches how taVNS is currently rated here.
items.summary: A PRISMA-ScR scoping review and evidence map of noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation across otolaryngology, which — for the first time in one place — quantifies the size and quality of the field: 20 included studies, of which 8 concern tinnitus, all judged largely exploratory. It adds no new patient data and no pooled effect estimates. 4974 records identified, 2690 unique records screened, 20 studies included; indication categories: tinnitus n=8, dysphagia n=3, vestibular disorders/rehabilitation n=3, Menière's disease n=2, olfactory dysfunction n=2, pharyngeal dysesthesia n=1, LPR-related disorders n=1. No pooled effect sizes reported.

detail.population: Published human clinical studies (RCTs, non-randomized trials, cohorts, mechanistic analyses, case series) of noninvasive VNS in otolaryngologic indications; tinnitus was the largest single indication cluster
detail.sampleSize: 20 included studies (8 tinnitus) from 2690 unique records screened; patient numbers not reported in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: Descriptive mapping of reported human clinical evidence on nVNS across a predefined otolaryngology outcome-domain framework (no efficacy endpoint)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Identification of methodological gaps: sample size, comparator/blinding strategy, stimulation-parameter harmonization, follow-up duration, harms reporting
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — a scoping review with no pooled or extracted psychoacoustic loudness-matching data; it makes no claim about the tinnitus percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — outcomes across included studies were described as 'primarily patient-reported' but no pooled distress effect (THI/TFI/TQ) is reported, and the authors explicitly state the evidence does not establish clinical effectiveness.
detail.otherOutcomes: Notes that vestibular rehabilitation and dysphagia studies more often used operationalizable functional endpoints than tinnitus studies did; no sleep/QoL synthesis reported
detail.safety: No new safety data generated; the review reports that harms were heterogeneously reported across the 20 included studies, which is itself a documentation gap rather than a signal
limitations: Scoping review by design — no risk-of-bias appraisal, no pooled analysis, no GRADE rating
No effect sizes, confidence intervals or per-study sample sizes in the abstract record
Tinnitus findings not separated by loudness vs distress outcomes
Included literature itself has small samples, variable blinding/sham, non-harmonized stimulation parameters, short follow-up
Single-centre author group; no reported protocol registration in the available record
detail.funding: independent — all three authors are from a single hospital otolaryngology department in Wuxi, China, and declare no competing interests; no funding source stated and no device manufacturer involvement disclosed
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small uncontrolled study measures blood-flow changes during acupuncture for tinnitus; tinnitus scores did not track them
items.whyMatters: This 10-patient retrospective study looked at whether devices measuring blood flow could track what acupuncture and moxibustion do in people with tinnitus. It found short-term circulation changes, but tinnitus handicap scores did not consistently follow them, so it is not evidence that acupuncture helps tinnitus.
items.summary: A small retrospective case series (n=10) applying acceleration photoplethysmography and pulsed-wave Doppler of the superficial temporal artery as objective hemodynamic monitors during acupuncture plus moxibustion for subjective tinnitus. The novelty is the measurement approach, not any demonstration of tinnitus benefit — and the authors explicitly note THI changes did not consistently track the hemodynamic changes. none reported (abstract states c/a ratio increased significantly after acupuncture, and PSV, EDV and MV significantly increased while RI decreased in the superficial temporal artery, without numeric values or effect sizes; no THI numbers given)

detail.population: Patients with subjective tinnitus treated with acupuncture and moxibustion at a Korean Medicine clinic (Dongguk University); further demographic and tinnitus-duration details not given in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: Change in hemodynamic measures — acceleration photoplethysmogram (APG) indices (notably c/a ratio) and pulsed-wave Doppler parameters (PSV, EDV, MV, RI) of the superficial temporal artery — before vs after treatment
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) scores, reported only as not consistently aligning with hemodynamic changes
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating of the tinnitus percept was reported at all; blood-flow parameters say nothing about the percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI was collected but no group-level change is reported, and the authors state THI changes did not consistently align with the hemodynamic findings; with n=10, no control and no randomization, no distress conclusion can be drawn.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse events or tolerability data described for acupuncture or moxibustion in this retrospective review
limitations: Retrospective chart review, n=10
No control or sham group; acute pre/post within-subject comparison only
No randomization and no blinding
Acupuncture and moxibustion given together — effects cannot be attributed to either
No numeric effect sizes or THI values reported in the abstract
Hemodynamic measures are surrogate markers with unestablished relationship to tinnitus perception
No follow-up duration stated; changes appear acute
Multiple hemodynamic parameters tested, raising multiplicity concerns
Single-center Korean Medicine department; likely selection bias in charts reviewed
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest; all from the College of Korean Medicine, Dongguk University, which has a disciplinary stake in acupuncture/moxibustion. Funding source not stated in the record provided.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Hyperacusis found in 16.5% of chronic tinnitus patients and linked to much higher tinnitus handicap
items.whyMatters: People whose tinnitus comes with sound sensitivity report far more disruption to daily life, so clinicians should check for hyperacusis routinely. This is an observational snapshot, not a test of any treatment.
items.summary: A single-centre Serbian cross-sectional series of 194 chronic subjective tinnitus patients reporting a hyperacusis prevalence of 16.5% (by structured interview plus uncomfortable loudness level measurement) and a large difference in tinnitus handicap between those with and without hyperacusis (THI 76.3 vs 41.9). The association itself is already well established; the contribution is another prevalence estimate at the low end of the published range, using objective ULLs alongside interview. Hyperacusis in 32/194 (16.5%); THI 76.3 (T+H) vs 41.9 (T), p < 0.001; significantly lower ULLs in the hyperacusis group (p < 0.001; exact values not given in abstract)

detail.population: Adults aged 21–85 years with chronic subjective tinnitus attending ENT clinics in Serbia; 32 with hyperacusis (T+H), 162 without (T)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Prevalence of hyperacusis among chronic subjective tinnitus patients, and its association with Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) scores
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Uncomfortable loudness levels (ULLs), degree of hearing loss, self-reported daily functioning
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational study with no intervention; ULL measures tolerance of EXTERNAL sound (a hyperacusis measure) and says nothing about the loudness of the tinnitus percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — the large THI gap is a cross-sectional association between comorbid hyperacusis and tinnitus handicap, not evidence that any treatment reduces distress.
detail.otherOutcomes: Hearing loss degree and daily functioning were assessed, but no separable numerical results are given in the abstract beyond the THI and ULL comparisons.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational study with no intervention.
limitations: Cross-sectional design: cannot establish direction of causation between hyperacusis and higher tinnitus handicap

Hyperacusis defined by a non-standardised structured clinical interview rather than a validated instrument (e.g. Khalfa HQ), and no stated ULL cut-off, so the 16.5% prevalence is not comparable across studies
Highly unbalanced groups (32 vs 162) and no adjustment reported for age, hearing loss, tinnitus duration or psychiatric comorbidity
Single-country clinic sample — referral/selection bias toward more severe cases
Prevalence sits well below many published estimates (often 40%+), suggesting definition-dependence rather than a settled figure
No treatment or follow-up data
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest; academic/hospital affiliations only, no manufacturer involvement stated. No funding source given in the record.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small Swiss study: people with tinnitus were slower at identifying certain speech sounds in noise, but no less accurate
items.whyMatters: It adds to evidence that tinnitus may involve subtle problems with timing in how the brain handles sound, even when hearing tests look normal. It is a mechanism study in 49 people — it does not test or support any treatment.
items.summary: A small case-control psychoacoustic study in normal-hearing adults reports that chronic tinnitus is associated with slower plosive (temporal-cue) phoneme identification in noise (+89 ms) without accuracy loss, while fricative (spectral-cue) discrimination is intact — suggesting a selective temporal-processing deficit rather than a general speech-in-noise deficit. Fricatives in noise: accuracy 0.69 (tinnitus) vs 0.73 (controls), model-based group contrast p=0.778. Plosives in noise: accuracy 0.47 vs 0.49, p=0.212; reaction time +89 ms slower in tinnitus, p=0.002. Speed-accuracy trade-off present in controls (p<0.001), absent in tinnitus.

detail.population: 49 normal-hearing adults (26 with chronic subjective tinnitus, 23 matched controls) with matched audiometric thresholds and supra-threshold processing, recruited at University Hospital Zurich
detail.primaryEndpoint: Phoneme identification accuracy and reaction time in a two-alternative forced-choice task with fricative (/s, ʃ/) and plosive (/pʰ, t/) contrasts, in quiet and individualized noise
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Speed-accuracy trade-off analysis; cognitive measures (no significant group differences reported)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this study made no measurement of tinnitus loudness or of any change in the percept; it is a speech-perception experiment, not a treatment or psychoacoustic loudness study.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life outcomes were reported.
detail.otherOutcomes: Hearing: groups were matched on audiometric thresholds and supra-threshold processing by design; cognitive measures showed no significant group differences.
detail.safety: Not reported — non-interventional listening experiment, no safety outcomes applicable.
limitations: Small sample (26 vs 23), cross-sectional case-control design — no causal inference
Only normal-hearing participants; results may not generalize to the majority of tinnitus patients who have hearing loss
Single fricative and single plosive contrast tested; narrow stimulus set
Reaction-time effect found on one of several contrasts/conditions — risk of selective/multiple-comparison findings
No reported association with tinnitus loudness, duration, laterality or distress scores
Plosive accuracy near chance-to-low levels (0.47–0.49), complicating interpretation of the RT difference
Funding and COI statements not visible in the retrieved record
detail.funding: unclear — academic authors (University Hospital Zurich / University of Zurich); no funding or competing-interest statement available in the retrieved PubMed record. No manufacturer involvement apparent.
detail.source: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Tinnitus distress questionnaires overlap substantially with depression questionnaires, content analysis finds
items.whyMatters: Common tinnitus questionnaires ask about sleep, energy, concentration and mood — the same things depression questionnaires ask about — so a score that improves may reflect better mood rather than a change in the tinnitus itself. The overlap differs a lot between instruments (lowest for the TQ, highest for the TRQ), which matters when comparing results across studies.
items.summary: First systematic ICF-based content analysis quantifying how much the items of six standard tinnitus distress questionnaires (THI, TQ, mTQ, THQ, TRQ, TFI) overlap in content with seven depression questionnaires, showing overlap ranges from ~12% (TQ) to ~73% (TRQ). It is a measurement/construct-validity paper, not treatment evidence. Depression questionnaires covered 14 second-level ICF categories vs 23 for tinnitus distress questionnaires. Seven categories were shared: energy and drive, sleep, attention, emotional, thought functions, interpersonal interactions and relationships, recreation and leisure. Overlap with depression instruments: TQ lowest at 11.54–26.92%, TRQ highest at 61.54–73.08%. Among depression scales: SDS least overlap with tinnitus scales (40–60%), DASS-42 depression subscale most (85.71–100%).

detail.population: No human participants — the units of analysis were validated self-report instruments: 6 tinnitus distress questionnaires (THI, TQ, mTQ, THQ, TRQ, TFI) and 7 depressive symptom questionnaires (BDI-II, HADS-D, SDS, PHQ-9, CES-D, SCL-90-R depression subscale, DASS-42 depression subscale)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Degree of content overlap between tinnitus distress and depressive symptom questionnaires, measured as shared second-level ICF categories after linking all items with established ICF linking rules
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Breadth of ICF category coverage per questionnaire type; identification of which specific ICF domains are shared
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this study does not measure or address the loudness of the tinnitus percept at all; it analyzes questionnaire item content only.
detail.distressOutcome: none — it examines how distress is *measured* and how far those measures contaminate with depression content; it reports no treatment effect on distress in any patient.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported (no clinical outcomes; sleep, energy and interpersonal function appear only as ICF content categories present in the instruments)
detail.safety: Not reported — no human subjects and no interventions involved.
limitations: Content/construct analysis only — no patient data, no psychometric or empirical correlation data
ICF linking involves subjective judgment; inter-rater reliability and linking procedure detail not summarized in the abstract
Analysis restricted to second-level ICF categories, which may exaggerate or blur overlap compared with third-level granularity
Only 13 instruments included; excludes other widely used measures (e.g. TFI subscale-level analysis, mini-TQ variants, generic QoL tools)
Says nothing about whether overlap actually biases trial results in practice — that would require empirical data
detail.funding: unclear — authors declare no competing interests, but one co-author (Assouly) lists an affiliation with Cochlear Technology Centre (Mechelen), a hearing-device manufacturer. No manufacturer product is evaluated here, so the risk of bias on the reported content analysis is low, but the affiliation should be noted.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: US military trial recruiting to test whether PTSD therapy or tinnitus CBT should come first
items.whyMatters: Many veterans have both PTSD and tinnitus, and clinicians currently have no evidence on which condition to treat first. This government-funded trial is enrolling 160 people to answer that question, but results are not expected until around 2028.
items.summary: A routine ClinicalTrials.gov update (status RECRUITING, last updated 2026-09-25) for NCT07106593, a DoD-funded randomized sequencing trial testing whether Cognitive Processing Therapy for PTSD should precede CBT for tinnitus, or vice versa, in service members/veterans with mild TBI-related tinnitus and comorbid PTSD. No results are posted; start was August 2025 with estimated completion August 2028.

detail.population: Adult active-duty military personnel and veterans with diagnosed PTSD, at least one mild TBI, and chronic bothersome subjective tinnitus at least possibly related to head injury; seen at UT Health San Antonio
detail.primaryEndpoint: Co-primary: PTSD Checklist (PTSD symptoms) and Tinnitus Functional Index (tinnitus-related distress), baseline to 6-month follow-up (~12 months)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported in the registry record; pre/post functional MRI is described as an exploratory neurobiological aim in willing participants
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating is listed among the outcomes; both primary measures (PCL, TFI) are symptom/distress questionnaires, and nothing here speaks to the tinnitus percept itself.
detail.distressOutcome: none — TFI is a co-primary distress outcome, but the trial is only recruiting and has reported no data, so it provides no distress evidence at this time.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported (fMRI-based neurobiological markers are an exploratory aim; no data available)
detail.safety: Not reported; the record notes a Data Monitoring Committee is in place and the interventions are non-drug, non-device behavioral therapies.
limitations: No results posted — recruiting only, primary completion estimated August 2028
Single-site trial (San Antonio) with one academic collaborator, limiting generalizability
Both arms receive both active treatments, so it tests sequencing rather than efficacy versus any control; no waitlist or sham arm
Only the outcomes assessor is masked; participants and therapists are unblinded, as is unavoidable in psychotherapy trials
Highly selected population (military/veteran, mTBI-related, PTSD-comorbid tinnitus) may not generalize to general tinnitus clinic patients
Registry-described 'crossover' is really a sequential design; carryover between phases will complicate interpretation
No loudness or psychoacoustic outcome measures at all
detail.funding: independent — lead sponsor is UT Health Science Center at San Antonio with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign as collaborator; funded by DoD CDMRP (HT9425-24-1-0988). No device or pharmaceutical manufacturer involvement is listed; not FDA-regulated drug or device.
detail.source: The University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Singapore neuronavigated rTMS tinnitus trial suspended for staffing reasons; no results reported
items.whyMatters: A small Singapore trial testing MRI-guided repetitive magnetic brain stimulation for tinnitus has paused recruitment because its lead investigator is away and staffing is short — not because of any safety or effectiveness problem. Nothing about how well rTMS works for tinnitus has changed.
items.summary: A registry status change only: the Singapore neuronavigated rTMS crossover trial (NCT07435298) has been SUSPENDED, with the stated reason being that the principal investigator is on overseas training and there is insufficient manpower; recruitment is expected to resume on the PI's return. No results, no enrollment data, no efficacy or safety findings are reported.

detail.population: Adults 21-80 with chronic subjective tinnitus (T-VAS ≥1/10 in any domain: sound, distress, or QoL), excluding major depression, psychotic history, epilepsy, MRI contraindications
detail.primaryEndpoint: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) at weeks 0, 3, 6 and 7 — a distress/handicap measure, not loudness
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) and Tinnitus-Visual Analogue Scale (T-VAS, which includes a loudness/sound domain) at the same four timepoints
detail.comparisonType: Not reported — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no data exist; the only loudness-adjacent measure (T-VAS sound domain) is a secondary self-rating and no results have been posted.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI/TFI are the primary and secondary endpoints but no outcome data have been reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — the trial lists establishing safety and tolerability of neuronavigated TMS as an aim, but no adverse event data are available and the suspension is explicitly administrative (PI overseas, manpower shortage), not safety-related.
limitations: No results reported; registry status change only
Suspension is administrative (PI abroad, staffing), so the trial may or may not resume as planned
Design internal inconsistency: intervention model description says 'open-label' while masking is recorded as DOUBLE (participant and outcomes assessor)
90° coil-tilt sham is a weak sham — it can differ in scalp sensation and is a known blinding weakness in rTMS trials
Crossover with only a 2-week washout risks carryover of rTMS effects, which can persist longer
Primary endpoint is THI (distress/handicap); loudness is captured only by a secondary single-item VAS, not psychoacoustic loudness matching
Very permissive inclusion (T-VAS ≥1/10) may enrol minimally affected patients, limiting room for improvement
Estimated n=50 is small; no primary completion until October 2027
detail.funding: independent — lead sponsor National University Hospital, Singapore, with Alexandra Hospital as collaborator; no device manufacturer funding declared in the record. Not FDA-regulated drug or device per the record.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.
